findings.title: K000156741: BIG-IP APM vulnerability CVE-2025-53521 (F5 Security Advisory)
findings.summary_md: F5 published advisory K000156741 on October 15, 2025 (page shows Published Date Oct 15, 2025, Updated Date Apr 1, 2026) for a CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow, internal ID 1977933, in the BIG-IP APM apmd process, reachable unauthenticated on the data plane when an access policy is configured on a virtual server. The bug was originally remediated as a DoS issue at CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) and re-categorized in March 2026 to critical RCE at 9.8 (v3.1) / 9.3 (v4.0) once F5 learned it had been exploited, with fixes in 17.5.1.3, 17.1.3, 16.1.6.1, and 15.1.10.8. F5 lists no mitigation, credits Schuberg Philis, Bart Vrancken, Fox-IT, and the Dutch NCSC, and warns that UCS backups taken from compromised systems can contain persistent malware.

findings.title: CISA adds one known exploited vulnerability to catalog (CVE-2025-53521)
findings.summary_md: CISA added CVE-2025-53521 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on March 27, 2026, based on evidence of active exploitation, and ordered federal agencies to secure their BIG-IP APM systems by midnight on Monday, March 30, 2026. The required action is to apply mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinue use of the product.

findings.title: Hackers exploiting critical F5 BIG-IP flaw in attacks, patch now
findings.summary_md: BleepingComputer reported on March 30, 2026 that F5 reclassified CVE-2025-53521 from DoS to critical RCE and warned that attackers were using it to deploy webshells on unpatched devices, with indicators published in K000160486. The article cites Shadowserver tracking over 240,000 BIG-IP instances exposed online at the time, and notes F5 advised defenders to check disks, logs, and terminal history for signs of malicious activity.

findings.title: ESET names PoisonedRefresh after finding installer and payload on VirusTotal
findings.summary_md: ESET Research reported on April 24, 2026 that it had discovered two related malware components on VirusTotal roughly a month after F5's c05d5254 advisory and named the threat PoisonedRefresh. The post describes a umount installer that prepends a malicious ELF to /usr/sbin/httpd when run as root with a first argument under /mnt/tm_install, disables SELinux, and also infects umount, httpd, and rc.local inside the install media so the malware persists and spreads to other BIG-IP systems. ESET shared SHA1 hashes as IoCs and declined to attribute, noting the access vector suggests a sophisticated actor.

findings.title: Dissecting a PHP web server rootkit (Sophos X-Ops)
findings.summary_md: Sophos X-Ops published the second-stage analysis on September 7, 2026, one day before this story's coverage: the sample hides strings with RC4, intercepts __libc_start_main to run before main(), hooks the APR module loader apr_dso_load to wait for libphp, and prepends a PHP web shell to the in-memory view of apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, and webtop_popup_css.php3 via mmap() interception, leaving disk files clean. The shell executes eval() on requests carrying the magic prefix BSOHAzPB and returns HTTP 201 with Content-Type text/css, while a separate AF_UNIX socket at /run/bigtlog.pipe authenticates with the token Kzwd6jM5 and redirects streams into /bin/bash without any TCP listener. Sophos correlates the payload with the umount installer via a matching 0x5430 malicious prefix on infected httpd, detects the analyzed sample (SHA-256 26bd5b0722d1dbab5db749a063c49bc8638653ac2addfead7a9cb3d6d57bccc9) as Linux/Agnt-IC, and credits ESET's parallel analysis under the PoisonedRefresh name.
